etymology: From Old French rober, to plunder, of Germanic origin (compare reave, bereave). Webster 1828: deprived of by force or stealth; plundered. Scripture’s most startling use has God as the victim and His own people as the thieves.
biblical_def: Malachi puts the charge as a question no Israelite would have expected: Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings (Malachi 3:8). The withholding of what is owed is not merely stinginess; it is theft, and the injured party is the Almighty. Note the reply the people give — Wherein have we robbed thee? — the settled unconsciousness of a nation that has redefined its duty downward until the shortfall no longer registers. Judgment, when it comes, takes the same form: this is a people robbed and spoiled; they are all of them snared in holes, and they are hid in prison houses: they are for a prey, and none delivereth (Isaiah 42:22). What Israel did to God is done to Israel, and no one restores. Paul uses the word of himself with deliberate roughness, to shame the Corinthians for what they had left him to do: I robbed other churches, taking wages of them, to do you service (2 Corinthians 11:8). He had taken support from poorer congregations in order to preach free of charge to a rich one, and he calls it robbery to make the point sting.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ROB as to take from another by force or by stealth; to plunder; to strip unlawfully; hence ROBBED, deprived by force or theft; plundered; stripped.
webster_full: ROB, v.t. — To take from another by force or by stealth; to seize and carry away by violence.
To plunder; to strip unlawfully; as, to rob a house.
To take away by oppression or injustice; to deprive of what is due.
ROBBED, pp. — Deprived by theft or force; plundered; stripped.
Old French rober, of Germanic origin; the same root as reave and bereave.
scriptures: Malachi 3:8
Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings.
Isaiah 42:22
But this is a people robbed and spoiled; they are all of them snared in holes, and they are hid in prison houses: they are for a prey, and none delivereth; for a spoil, and none saith, Restore.
2 Corinthians 11:8
I robbed other churches, taking wages of them, to do you service.
Proverbs 22:22
Rob not the poor, because he is poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate:
corruption_summary: Malachi 3 is the standing proof-text of the prosperity teachers, who read the promised blessing as a guaranteed financial return; the passage is a covenant lawsuit against theft, and its promise is God’s faithfulness, not a rate of interest.
corruption_paragraphs: The seed-faith industry has built a great deal on Malachi 3:10, and the reading fails on the text’s own terms. Malachi is a covenant lawsuit. The nation stands accused of robbery, the charge is specified as tithes and offerings, and the invitation to prove me now herewith is God vindicating His own faithfulness against a people who had concluded it was vain to serve Him (Malachi 3:14). To turn that into a technique — give in order to receive, and the more given the more returned — reverses the parties. It makes the giver the initiator and God the respondent, which is precisely the structure of pagan sacrifice. The Reformed doctrine of stewardship holds the opposite: the earth is the LORD’s and the fulness thereof, the giver returns what was never his, and the blessing promised is covenantal, not commercial.

The most searching phrase in the passage is the people’s answer: Wherein have we robbed thee? They were not defiant; they were unaware. This is the ordinary condition of a conscience that has adjusted its standard slowly, and it is why the objective, external word of God must judge the heart rather than the heart judging itself. Jeremiah 17:9 states the principle and the Reformed doctrine of total depravity applies it to the whole man, mind and will included. A man does not merely sin; he becomes unable to see accurately that he is sinning. Proverbs 22:22 shows the other direction of the same offence — robbing the poor because he is poor, that is, because he cannot retaliate — and Scripture answers it by naming the LORD as the one who will plead their cause.
roots_summary: Hebrew qaba (H6906), to rob or defraud; gazal (H1497), to tear away, to seize by violence; shasas (H8154), to plunder; Greek sulao (G4813), to strip or rob.
roots_lines: Hebrew qaba (H6906) — to rob or defraud; the rare verb of the charge in Malachi 3:8.
Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear away, to seize by violence; Rob not the poor (Proverbs 22:22).
Hebrew shasah (H8154) — to spoil or plunder; a people robbed and spoiled (Isaiah 42:22).
Greek sulao (G4813) — to strip, to despoil; Paul’s deliberately harsh word in 2 Corinthians 11:8.
Hebrew maaser (H4643) — the tithe, the tenth part withheld in Malachi’s indictment.
usage: Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me (Malachi 3:8) — withholding what is owed is theft, and the injured party is the Almighty.
Wherein have we robbed thee? (Malachi 3:8) — the settled unconsciousness of a people whose standard has drifted.
I robbed other churches, taking wages of them, to do you service (2 Corinthians 11:8) — Paul chooses a harsh word on purpose.

etymology: From Old French chacier, to hunt or pursue, from Latin captare, to try to seize. Webster 1828: pursued; hunted; driven. In the covenant curses the terror of being chased is inflicted without any pursuer at all.
biblical_def: Leviticus 26 sets out what covenant unfaithfulness will cost, and the most frightening clause in it involves no army: I will send a faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies; and the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them; and they shall flee, as fleeing from a sword; and they shall fall when none pursueth (Leviticus 26:36). God does not need to send a pursuer; He withdraws courage, and a falling leaf finishes the work. Moses states the arithmetic of the reverse case, where the chasing is Israel’s and the ratio is impossible: How should one chase a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, except their Rock had sold them, and the LORD had shut them up? (Deuteronomy 32:30). Victory and defeat alike are traced to the same hand. Bildad, wrong about Job but right about the wicked in general, describes the end: He shall be driven from light into darkness, and chased out of the world (Job 18:18). And Isaiah likens scattered Babylon to game: it shall be as the chased roe, and as a sheep that no man taketh up (Isaiah 13:14).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CHASE as to pursue for the purpose of taking; to hunt; to drive away, to put to flight; hence CHASED, pursued, hunted, driven, put to flight.
webster_full: CHASE, v.t. — To pursue for the purpose of taking, as game; to hunt.
To pursue, or drive, as a defeated enemy; to put to flight.
To drive away; to dispel; as, to chase away care.
CHASED, pp. — Pursued; sought; driven; dispelled; put to flight.
Old French chacier, from Latin captare, frequentative of capio, to take — the same root as catch and capture.
scriptures: Leviticus 26:36

And upon them that are left alive of you I will send a faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies; and the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them; and they shall flee, as fleeing from a sword; and they shall fall when none pursueth.
Deuteronomy 32:30
How should one chase a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, except their Rock had sold them, and the LORD had shut them up?
He shall be driven from light into darkness, and chased out of the world.
Proverbs 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
corruption_summary: Leviticus 26:36 and Proverbs 28:1 diagnose fear as a moral condition under God’s hand, which the therapeutic account of anxiety as a purely clinical event cannot supply.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture is not indifferent to bodily affliction, and this dictionary does not deny that fear has physical causes or that lawful means may treat them. But Leviticus 26:36 describes a fear that is judicial: God sends a faintness of heart, and the sound of a leaf does the rest. Proverbs 28:1 states the same principle as a proverb — The wicked flee when no man pursueth — and pairs it with the boldness of the righteous. The modern therapeutic frame, which treats anxiety exclusively as a disorder to be managed and never as a condition that might be addressed by repentance and the fear of God, is not a neutral advance in knowledge; it is an anthropology, and it has quietly replaced a biblical one. Where guilt is the cause, only forgiveness is the cure, and no technique will reach it.

Deuteronomy 32:30 guards the doctrine of providence at its hardest point: defeat. Moses does not permit Israel to explain a rout by enemy strength or by tactical error. Except their Rock had sold them, and the LORD had shut them up — the cause is God’s judicial hand, and the same hand gives the impossible victories elsewhere in the book. This is the Reformed doctrine of providence extending to second causes and to evil suffered, without making God the author of sin. The 1689 Confession states it carefully: God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, yet so as the contingency of second causes is not taken away. A providence that governs only the pleasant half of history is not the providence of Scripture, and it will fail the believer exactly when he needs it.
roots_summary: Hebrew radaph (H7291), to pursue or chase; nadad (H5074), to flee or wander; nus (H5127), to flee; Greek dioko (G1377), to pursue, to persecute.
roots_lines: Hebrew radaph (H7291) — to pursue, to chase; the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them (Leviticus 26:36).
Hebrew nus (H5127) — to flee; they shall flee, as fleeing from a sword (Leviticus 26:36).
Hebrew nadad (H5074) — to wander or be chased away; used of the fugitive wicked (Job 18:18).
Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, and so to persecute; the New Testament counterpart of radaph.
Hebrew tsebi (H6643) — the roe or gazelle; as the chased roe (Isaiah 13:14).
usage: The sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them (Leviticus 26:36) — God withdraws courage, and a falling leaf finishes the work.
Except their Rock had sold them (Deuteronomy 32:30) — defeat is traced to the same hand that gives victory.
The wicked flee when no man pursueth (Proverbs 28:1) — guilt supplies its own pursuer.

etymology: From Latin violentus, forcible, vehement, from vis, force. Webster 1828: forcible; acting with physical strength; moving or acting with vehemence. In Scripture the word is almost always a verdict on a man’s character, and it recoils on the man who earns it.
biblical_def: The Psalter’s rule for the violent man is that his violence comes home: His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate (Psalm 7:16). The word pate is the crown of the head, and the image is a stone thrown upward. Proverbs identifies the violent man’s worst work as recruitment rather than assault: A violent man enticeth his neighbour, and leadeth him into the way that is not good (Proverbs 16:29) — he does not merely strike, he persuades. Against these stands the one text where violence is commended, and it is famously difficult: from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force (Matthew 11:12). Whatever else it means, it does not mean the kingdom is seized by human force in the ordinary sense; the surrounding context is John in prison and a generation that would neither dance nor mourn. The old Reformed reading takes it of the earnestness of those who press into the kingdom against every hindrance — men and women who will not be kept out. Isaiah gives the Servant’s contrast in one line: because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth (Isaiah 53:9).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines VIOLENT as forcible; acting with physical strength or vehemence; moving or acting with impetuosity; produced or effected by force; and, of persons, vehement, passionate, outrageous.
webster_full: VIOLENT, a. — Forcible; moving or acting with physical strength; urged or driven with force.
Vehement; outrageous; as a violent man; violent passions.
Produced or effected by force; not spontaneous; as a violent death.
Assailant; acting by force; not authorized; as violent measures.
Latin violentus, from vis, force, strength — the root also of violate and violence.
scriptures: Psalm 7:16
His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate.
Proverbs 16:29
A violent man enticeth his neighbour, and leadeth him into the way that is not good.
Matthew 11:12
And from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force.
Isaiah 53:9
And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.
corruption_summary: Two opposite errors work on this word: a triumphalist reading of Matthew 11:12 that licenses coercion for the kingdom, and a pacifist reading of Scripture that denies the civil magistrate the sword God gave him.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 11:12 has been pressed into service by movements that would advance the kingdom by force — the Munster radicals of the sixteenth century, and in another key the modern dominionist rhetoric that speaks of taking territory. The text will not bear it. Christ’s kingdom is not of this world and its weapons are not carnal (John 18:36; 2 Corinthians 10:4), and the Servant of Isaiah 53 is commended precisely for having done no violence. The historic Reformed reading, in Calvin and among the Puritans, is that the phrase describes the vehement earnestness of those pressing into the kingdom despite opposition, not a warrant for coercion. Whoever cites this verse to justify force against neighbours has read past the whole chapter, which ends with the Lord calling the heavy-laden to a yoke that is easy.

The opposite error is equally unbiblical. Romans 13:4 gives the civil magistrate the sword and calls him a minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil; the 1689 Confession affirms that magistracy is lawful and that Christians may serve in it and wage just war. A blanket pacifism that reads the Sermon on the Mount as abolishing the magistrate’s sword confuses the spheres God has distinguished. Personal vengeance is forbidden to the Christian; public justice is committed to the magistrate. Psalm 7:16 is the assurance that binds the two: the believer need not repay the violent man, because his violent dealing will come down upon his own pate whether by the magistrate now or by God at the last.
roots_summary: Hebrew chamas (H2555), violence, wrong, cruelty; arits (H6184), terrible, oppressive; Greek biazo (G971), to force or press; biastes (G973), a forceful man.
roots_lines: Hebrew chamas (H2555) — violence, wrong; the word that filled the earth before the flood (Genesis 6:11) and that the Servant had not done (Isaiah 53:9).
Hebrew arits (H6184) — terrible, violent, oppressive; used of the tyrant in Psalms and Isaiah.
Greek biazo (G971) — to force, to press violently; the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence (Matthew 11:12).
Greek biastes (G973) — a forceful or vehement man; the violent take it by force (Matthew 11:12).
Hebrew qodqod (H6936) — the crown of the head, the pate on which the violence descends (Psalm 7:16).
usage: His violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate (Psalm 7:16) — the stone thrown upward returns on the thrower.
A violent man enticeth his neighbour (Proverbs 16:29) — his worst work is recruitment, not assault.
Because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth (Isaiah 53:9) — the Servant’s contrast, and the ground of His innocence.

etymology: From Old French poison, a drink or potion, from Latin potio, a draught — a word for drink that narrowed to mean a deadly one. Webster 1828: any substance which, taken into the body, destroys life or impairs health. Scripture’s chief application is to the tongue.
biblical_def: Paul’s catena in Romans 3, assembling the Psalms into a single indictment of the race, spends four clauses on the organs of speech and ends here: Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips (Romans 3:13). The picture is exact — the venom sac of a serpent lies under the lip, so the poison is not an occasional lapse but a resident capacity, carried about and discharged at will. James reaches the same verdict from the pastoral side: But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison (James 3:8). Note no man: James has just observed that every kind of beast has been tamed by mankind, and then denies that the tongue can be added to the list. It is a doctrine of inability, not a counsel of effort. In the Song of Moses the poison belongs to the vine of a corrupt people: Their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps (Deuteronomy 32:33). Zophar completes the figure with the sinner’s own appetite: He shall suck the poison of asps: the viper's tongue shall slay him (Job 20:16).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines POISON as any substance which, when taken into the stomach, mixed with the blood, or applied to the skin, is capable of destroying life or impairing health; and figuratively, anything infectious or malignant to morals.
webster_full: POISON, n. — Any substance which, taken into the stomach or applied to the body, destroys life or impairs health; venom.
Anything infectious, malignant, or noxious to purity or happiness; as the poison of vice.
POISON, v.t. — To infect with anything fatal to life; to attack or destroy by poison.
To taint; to mar; to corrupt; as, to poison the mind.
Old French poison, a potion, from Latin potio, a drink — the same root as potion.
scriptures: Romans 3:13
Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips:
James 3:8
But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison.
Deuteronomy 32:33
Their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps.
He shall suck the poison of asps: the viper's tongue shall slay him.
corruption_summary: Romans 3:13 and James 3:8 together teach an inability of the whole man that no programme of communication skills can touch, and both texts are commonly softened into advice about being kinder with words.
corruption_paragraphs: James 3:8 is a doctrinal statement disguised as an observation. Having noted that every kind of beast, bird, serpent and sea creature has been tamed by mankind, James says the tongue cannot be. That is not hyperbole about difficulty; it is the doctrine of total depravity applied to speech. The tongue is a member of a fallen man, and it discharges what the heart contains — out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh (Matthew 12:34). Sermons that treat James 3 as a set of techniques for better communication invert the passage. The remedy for a poisoned tongue is a new heart, which only God gives; the taming James denies to man is exactly what regeneration begins and sanctification continues.

Romans 3:13 belongs to the argument that ends in Romans 3:19-20 with every mouth stopped and the whole world guilty. Paul is not describing the worst of men but the state of all men apart from grace, which is why he strings together Psalms 5, 140, 10 and Isaiah 59 and lets them speak as one voice. The modern instinct, in and out of the church, is to treat depravity as partial — a good nature spoiled at the edges, needing encouragement rather than resurrection. The Reformed doctrine is that the corruption reaches the whole man, mind and will included, and that the venom is under the lips, resident and ready, not visiting from outside. Only such a diagnosis makes sense of the remedy Paul announces three verses later.
roots_summary: Hebrew chemah (H2534), heat, venom, fury; rosh (H7219), a bitter or poisonous herb, gall; Greek ios (G2447), venom or rust; thanatephoros (G2287), death-bearing.
roots_lines: Greek ios (G2447) — venom, and also rust; the poison of asps is under their lips (Romans 3:13) and full of deadly poison (James 3:8).
Greek thanatephoros (G2287) — death-bearing, deadly; James’s adjective for the tongue’s venom (James 3:8).
Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, and so venom or fury; the poison of dragons (Deuteronomy 32:33).
Hebrew rosh (H7219) — a poisonous or bitter herb, gall; used of perverted justice in Amos 6:12.
Hebrew pethen (H6620) — the asp or cobra, the serpent whose venom supplies the figure (Job 20:16).
usage: The poison of asps is under their lips (Romans 3:13) — a resident capacity, carried about and discharged at will.
The tongue can no man tame (James 3:8) — a doctrine of inability, not a counsel of effort.
He shall suck the poison of asps (Job 20:16) — the sinner’s appetite for what will kill him.

etymology: From Latin rumor, a common talk, a report, through Old French rumour. Webster 1828: flying or popular report; a current story passing from one person to another without any known authority for its truth. Our Lord treats rumours as a permanent condition of the age, not a sign of its end.
biblical_def: The Olivet Discourse opens by lowering the temperature: And ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars: see that ye be not troubled: for all these things must come to pass, but the end is not yet (Matthew 24:6). Three things are said, and the church regularly keeps the first and loses the other two. There will be rumours; they are not to disturb you; and they do not mean the end has come. Christ’s pastoral aim is composure, not excitement. Jeremiah gives the same counsel to exiles who would hear alarming news year upon year: lest your heart faint, and ye fear for the rumour that shall be heard in the land; a rumour shall both come one year, and after that in another year shall come a rumour (Jeremiah 51:46). Ezekiel names the condition of a people under judgment as an unbroken succession of them: Mischief shall come upon mischief, and rumour shall be upon rumour; then shall they seek a vision of the prophet; but the law shall perish from the priest (Ezekiel 7:26) — when rumour multiplies, men go looking for new revelation and neglect the law they already have. Obadiah, by contrast, shows a report that is not rumour at all: We have heard a rumour from the LORD, and an ambassador is sent among the heathen (Obadiah 1:1).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines RUMOUR as flying or popular report; a current story passing from one person to another without any known authority for the truth of it; also, fame, report, or reputation.
webster_full: RUMOR, n. — Flying or popular report; a current story passing from one person to another without any known authority for its truth.
Report of a fact; a story well authorized. (An older and now rarer sense.)
Fame; reported celebrity; as, the rumor of his name.
RUMOR, v.t. — To report; to tell or circulate, as a report.
Latin rumor, a common talk; probably connected with a root meaning to murmur or roar.
scriptures: Matthew 24:6
And ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars: see that ye be not troubled: for all these things must come to pass, but the end is not yet.
Jeremiah 51:46

And lest your heart faint, and ye fear for the rumour that shall be heard in the land; a rumour shall both come one year, and after that in another year shall come a rumour, and violence in the land, ruler against ruler.
Ezekiel 7:26
Mischief shall come upon mischief, and rumour shall be upon rumour; then shall they seek a vision of the prophet; but the law shall perish from the priest, and counsel from the ancients.
Obadiah 1:1
The vision of Obadiah. Thus saith the Lord GOD concerning Edom; We have heard a rumour from the LORD, and an ambassador is sent among the heathen, Arise ye, and let us rise up against her in battle.
corruption_summary: Matthew 24:6 forbids the very use most often made of it: the treating of current wars and reports as a datable countdown, a habit inseparable from the dispensational prophecy industry.
corruption_paragraphs: Our Lord names wars and rumours of wars in order to say that they are not the sign — see that ye be not troubled... the end is not yet. The modern prophecy conference reverses the sentence, treating each headline as a countdown marker. That habit is inseparable from dispensational premillennialism, a nineteenth-century system (Darby, Scofield) unknown to any Reformation confession, which requires a detailed timetable and so must find one in the news. This dictionary rejects that system while leaving the millennial question itself open among the historic positions — amillennial, postmillennial, and historic premillennial. The practical damage is not merely intellectual: a church trained to scan the horizon for signs is a church distracted from the plain duties Christ actually assigns in the same discourse, which are watchfulness, faithfulness in service, and feeding the household in due season.

Ezekiel 7:26 traces the sequence exactly, and it is a warning to churches and not only to nations. When rumour piles on rumour, men seek a vision of the prophet while the law shall perish from the priest. Anxious times drive people toward new revelation and away from the settled word, which is the standing appetite behind every modern apostle-and-prophet movement — the New Apostolic Reformation, the prophetic conference circuit, the personal word delivered over the sure word written. This dictionary is cessationist with the Reformed mainstream: the canon is closed, and the remedy for a rumour-fed heart is not a fresh oracle but the law that has not perished and the ordinary means of grace.
roots_summary: Hebrew shemuah (H8052), a report or tidings; shema (H8088), a thing heard; Greek akoe (G189), a hearing, a report; pheme (G5345), fame or report.
roots_lines: Greek akoe (G189) — a hearing, and so a report; wars and rumours of wars (Matthew 24:6).
Hebrew shemuah (H8052) — a report, tidings, something heard; used of the rumours in Jeremiah 51:46 and Obadiah 1:1.
Hebrew shema (H8088) — a thing heard, a rumour; rumour shall be upon rumour (Ezekiel 7:26).
Greek pheme (G5345) — fame, report, the noun behind English fame.
Hebrew torah (H8451) — the law, the thing that perishes from the priest when rumour rules (Ezekiel 7:26).
usage: See that ye be not troubled... but the end is not yet (Matthew 24:6) — Christ’s pastoral aim is composure, not excitement.
Rumour shall be upon rumour... but the law shall perish from the priest (Ezekiel 7:26) — anxious men seek new revelation and neglect the word they have.
We have heard a rumour from the LORD (Obadiah 1:1) — a report with an author is not rumour at all.

etymology: From over and flow: to run over the brim or bank. Webster 1828: running over; abounding; exuberant; also, an inundation. Isaiah makes the overflowing flood his standing figure for an invasion that no treaty can divert.
biblical_def: Isaiah’s picture of judgment is water that will not respect an agreement. The rulers of Jerusalem had made a policy and boasted of it: We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us: for we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves (Isaiah 28:15). The reply, three verses on, is that the covenant with death shall be disannulled. Men do make arrangements with what will destroy them, and they call the arrangements security. The same prophet turns the figure on the LORD Himself, and it is more frightening still: his breath, as an overflowing stream, shall reach to the midst of the neck, to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity (Isaiah 30:28). Habakkuk sees the earth’s own reaction to God in motion: The mountains saw thee, and they trembled: the overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high (Habakkuk 3:10). And Job is asked who set the channels: Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, or a way for the lightning of thunder? (Job 38:25) — even the flood runs where it is told.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OVERFLOWING as running over, as a fluid; inundating; abounding; exuberant; and as a noun, an inundation, exuberance, or copiousness.
webster_full: OVERFLOW, v.t. — To spread over, as water; to inundate; to cover with water or other fluid.
To fill beyond the brim; to run over.
OVERFLOWING, ppr. — Spreading over, as a fluid; inundating; abounding.
OVERFLOWING, n. — An inundation; exuberance; copiousness; superabundance.
From over and flow, Anglo-Saxon oferflowan.
scriptures: Isaiah 28:15

Because ye have said, We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us: for we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves:
Isaiah 30:28

And his breath, as an overflowing stream, shall reach to the midst of the neck, to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity: and there shall be a bridle in the jaws of the people, causing them to err.
Habakkuk 3:10
The mountains saw thee, and they trembled: the overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high.
Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, or a way for the lightning of thunder;
corruption_summary: Isaiah 28:15 describes men sheltering under a refuge of lies and calling it prudence, which is the exact structure of every false assurance, religious or political.
corruption_paragraphs: We have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves. The rulers of Judah had not abandoned religion; they had arranged a policy — probably the Egyptian alliance — and taught themselves to regard it as safety. The phrase is one of the most useful in Scripture for exposing false assurance, because it names the mechanism: a man does not usually choose a lie knowing it to be one, he takes shelter in it and then defends the shelter. The Reformed doctrine of assurance is deliberately built against this. Assurance rests on the promises of God, the inward evidences of grace, and the testimony of the Spirit — not on a decision recorded, a ceremony undergone, or an alliance secured. The 1689 Confession warns that a man may deceive himself with false hopes and carnal presumptions, which is Isaiah 28 in confessional prose.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the same water which is judgment to the covenant-breaker is providence under God’s hand throughout. Job 38:25 asks who divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, and the expected answer governs everything: the flood does not escape God’s appointment, it runs in the channel He cut. Habakkuk sees the deep itself lift up its hands. Nothing in Scripture is a force loose from His government, which is why the believer under a rising flood is not being visited by chaos but is in the hands of the One who set the watercourse.
roots_summary: Hebrew shataph (H7857), to overflow, to rinse or overwhelm; sheteph (H7858), a flood or downpour; abar (H5674), to pass over or through.
roots_lines: Hebrew shataph (H7857) — to overflow, to overwhelm; the verb behind the overflowing scourge (Isaiah 28:15).
Hebrew sheteph (H7858) — a flood, an outpouring; the overflowing of waters (Job 38:25).
Hebrew nachal (H5158) — a torrent or wadi, a channel dry until the flood comes.
Hebrew abar (H5674) — to pass over or through; the scourge that shall pass through (Isaiah 28:15).
Hebrew shot (H7752) — a scourge or whip, joined to the flood image in Isaiah 28:15.
usage: When the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us (Isaiah 28:15) — men make arrangements with what will destroy them and call it security.
His breath, as an overflowing stream (Isaiah 30:28) — the figure turned upon the LORD Himself.
Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters? (Job 38:25) — even the flood runs where it is told.

etymology: From Middle English stampen, to pound or crush with the foot, of Germanic origin. Webster 1828: struck with the foot; impressed; crushed to powder. In Scripture the word belongs to two very different actions: the destruction of idols, and the trampling of a beast.
biblical_def: When Moses came down and dealt with the golden calf, he did not merely break it: I took your sin, the calf which ye had made, and burnt it with fire, and stamped it, and ground it very small, even until it was as small as dust: and I cast the dust thereof into the brook (Deuteronomy 9:21). Notice how Moses names the object — your sin, not your idol — and notice the thoroughness, which is the point: burnt, stamped, ground, cast into water. Josiah does the same to the grove: burned it at the brook Kidron, and stamped it small to powder, and cast the powder thereof upon the graves of the children of the people (2 Kings 23:6). Reformation in Scripture is never tidy or partial; the idol is reduced past the possibility of repair. The second use is terrible rather than righteous. Daniel’s fourth beast devoured and brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with the feet of it (Daniel 7:7) — what it cannot eat it treads. And Ezekiel is told to make the sign with his own body: Smite with thine hand, and stamp with thy foot, and say, Alas for all the evil abominations of the house of Israel! (Ezekiel 6:11).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines STAMP as to strike or beat forcibly with the bottom of the foot; to pound; to crush or bruise by beating; to impress with a mark; hence STAMPED, struck with the foot, impressed, crushed.
webster_full: STAMP, v.t. — To strike or beat forcibly with the bottom of the foot, or by thrusting the foot downward.
To impress with some mark or figure; as, to stamp a coin.
To pound; to bray; to crush or bruise by beating; as, to stamp to powder.
STAMPED, pp. — Struck with the foot; impressed; coined; crushed.
Middle English stampen, of Germanic origin; connected with step and with the German stampfen.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 9:21

And I took your sin, the calf which ye had made, and burnt it with fire, and stamped it, and ground it very small, even until it was as small as dust: and I cast the dust thereof into the brook that descended out of the mount.
2 Kings 23:6

And he brought out the grove from the house of the LORD, without Jerusalem, unto the brook Kidron, and burned it at the brook Kidron, and stamped it small to powder, and cast the powder thereof upon the graves of the children of the people.
Daniel 7:7

After this I saw in the night visions, and behold a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth: it devoured and brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with the feet of it: and it was diverse from all the beasts that were before it; and it had ten horns.
Ezekiel 6:11

Thus saith the Lord GOD; Smite with thine hand, and stamp with thy foot, and say, Alas for all the evil abominations of the house of Israel! for they shall fall by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence.
corruption_summary: Moses grinds the calf to dust rather than reforming its use, which is the opposite of the modern instinct to baptize a corrupt practice by giving it a Christian meaning.
corruption_paragraphs: The golden calf was not offered to a foreign god. Aaron had proclaimed a feast to the LORD (Exodus 32:5), and the people were worshipping the God of Israel by an image of their own devising. That is precisely why Moses destroys it utterly rather than repurposing it. The second commandment forbids not only the worship of false gods but the worship of the true God by images and inventions He has not appointed, and the regulative principle of worship follows directly: what Scripture commands is required, and what Scripture has not commanded is not permitted in corporate worship. The recurring proposal to take a practice drawn from elsewhere and sanctify it by intention is the calf argument, and Deuteronomy 9:21 is the answer to it — burnt, stamped, ground to dust, and thrown in the brook.

Josiah’s reformation shows the same thoroughness carried into a nation’s public life, and it is worth noticing where he scattered the powder: upon the graves of the common people who had sacrificed there. Reformation in Scripture is not merely the addition of true worship but the removal of false, and it costs something. Daniel 7:7 supplies the sober counterweight. The beast that stamps the residue is a picture of a power that recognizes no such limits at all, and Daniel’s vision ends not with the beast’s success but with the Ancient of days seated and the judgment set. This dictionary reads Daniel as sixth-century prophecy from the prophet whose name it bears, against the standard critical redating that turns predictive prophecy into after-the-fact composition.
roots_summary: Hebrew daqaq (H1854), to crush or beat small; kathath (H3807), to beat or pound; raphas (H7429), to trample; Aramaic rephas (H7512), to stamp with the feet.
roots_lines: Hebrew daqaq (H1854) — to crush fine, to beat small; the calf ground as small as dust (Deuteronomy 9:21).
Hebrew kathath (H3807) — to beat or pound to pieces; used of Josiah’s purge (2 Kings 23:6).
Aramaic rephas (H7512) — to trample, to stamp; the fourth beast stamped the residue (Daniel 7:7).
Hebrew raqa (H7554) — to beat out, to stamp with the foot; Ezekiel’s prophetic sign (Ezekiel 6:11).
Hebrew asherah (H842) — the grove or wooden image Josiah burned and stamped to powder (2 Kings 23:6).
usage: I took your sin, the calf which ye had made... and stamped it (Deuteronomy 9:21) — Moses names the object your sin, and reduces it past repair.
Stamped it small to powder (2 Kings 23:6) — reformation removes as well as adds, and it costs something.
Stamped the residue with the feet of it (Daniel 7:7) — what the beast cannot devour, it treads.

etymology: From Old French poulser, to thrust, from Latin pulsare, to beat or strike. Webster 1828: to press against with force; to drive by pressure. In Scripture it is a horn word — the action of a goring ox, and by extension the conquest of a nation.
biblical_def: The Hebrew verb belongs first to livestock, and the law is exact about the liability: If the ox shall push a manservant or a maidservant; he shall give unto their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned (Exodus 21:32). The sum is worth remembering — thirty pieces of silver, the price the law set on a slave gored by a beast, and the price at which the Son of God was sold. From the ox the figure passes to the nation. Moses blesses Joseph with horns: his horns are like the horns of unicorns: with them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth: and they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh (Deuteronomy 33:17). Daniel sees the Medo-Persian empire in exactly this posture: I saw the ram pushing westward, and northward, and southward; so that no beasts might stand before him... but he did according to his will, and became great (Daniel 8:4) — and the following verses bring the he-goat that breaks him, for the ram’s own will is not the last word. The word is also the vehicle of false prophecy: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made him horns of iron: and he said, Thus saith the LORD, With these shalt thou push the Syrians, until thou have consumed them (1 Kings 22:11).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PUSH as to press against with force; to drive or impel by pressure; to thrust, as with a pointed instrument or with the horns, as an ox.
webster_full: PUSH, v.t. — To press against with force; to drive or impel by pressure.
To butt; to thrust with the horns or with a pointed instrument; as, an ox pushes with his horns.
To press or urge forward; as, to push an objection too far.
PUSH, n. — A thrust; a pressure; an assault or attack; an effort.
Old French poulser, from Latin pulsare, to beat — the root also of pulse and repulse.
scriptures: Exodus 21:32
If the ox shall push a manservant or a maidservant; he shall give unto their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned.
Deuteronomy 33:17

His glory is like the firstling of his bullock, and his horns are like the horns of unicorns: with them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth: and they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh.
Daniel 8:4

I saw the ram pushing westward, and northward, and southward; so that no beasts might stand before him, neither was there any that could deliver out of his hand; but he did according to his will, and became great.
1 Kings 22:11
And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made him horns of iron: and he said, Thus saith the LORD, With these shalt thou push the Syrians, until thou have consumed them.
corruption_summary: Zedekiah’s iron horns are the model of confident false prophecy — a dramatic sign, the formula Thus saith the LORD, four hundred agreeing voices, and a message that was simply untrue.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Kings 22 is the fullest case study of false prophecy in the Old Testament, and every mark of it is present. Zedekiah has a visual aid, the correct formula (Thus saith the LORD), overwhelming numerical support, and a message the king wanted. Micaiah has none of these and is imprisoned for saying so. The chapter is decisive against the assumption that consensus, sincerity or spiritual impressiveness authenticate a word from God; the only test Scripture gives is agreement with what God has already spoken, and the outcome in Deuteronomy 18:22. This is why the dictionary is cessationist and holds the canon closed. Modern prophetic ministries that issue predictions, revise them, and continue without repentance are operating in Zedekiah’s line, and the fact that some of them are warm and evidently sincere is exactly what the chapter warns will be the case.

Exodus 21:32 sets thirty shekels of silver as the compensation for a slave gored by an ox, and Zechariah 11:12-13 has the LORD Himself appraised at that goodly price, and Matthew 26:15 records the bargain struck. Scripture is deliberate about this figure. It is not a coincidence to be admired but a valuation to be felt: the priests of Israel priced the Son of God at the statutory rate for damaged property. The typology runs through the law rather than around it, which is a standing argument against the habit of treating the Mosaic case laws as culturally expired curiosities. They are the vocabulary in which the New Testament states the worth of Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew nagach (H5055), to butt or gore with the horn; qeren (H7161), a horn; Greek keratizo, to gore; the ram of Daniel 8 is Aramaic-era Hebrew ayil (H352).
roots_lines: Hebrew nagach (H5055) — to gore or push with the horn; used of the ox (Exodus 21:32), Joseph (Deuteronomy 33:17) and the ram (Daniel 8:4).
Hebrew qeren (H7161) — a horn, the standing biblical figure for strength and dominion.
Hebrew reem (H7214) — the wild ox, rendered unicorn in the Authorized Version (Deuteronomy 33:17).
Hebrew ayil (H352) — a ram; the Medo-Persian empire in Daniel’s vision (Daniel 8:4, 8:20).
Hebrew sheqel (H8255) — the shekel; thirty of them the price of a gored servant (Exodus 21:32).
usage: If the ox shall push a manservant... thirty shekels of silver (Exodus 21:32) — the statutory price the priests later set on Christ.
With them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth (Deuteronomy 33:17) — the horn as the figure of dominion.
With these shalt thou push the Syrians (1 Kings 22:11) — a dramatic sign, the right formula, and a false word.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon thrawan, to twist or hurl. Webster 1828: to fling, cast, or hurl; to drive or send by force. In the prophets it is chiefly a demolition word — God’s commission to His servants regularly begins with what must come down.
biblical_def: Gideon’s call to public service does not begin with Midian; it begins with his father’s altar: the LORD said unto him, Take thy father's young bullock, even the second bullock of seven years old, and throw down the altar of Baal that thy father hath, and cut down the grove that is by it (Judges 6:25). Reformation starts at home and it starts with removal. Jeremiah’s commission has six verbs, and four of them are demolition: I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant (Jeremiah 1:10). The order matters; nothing is built on the site until the site is cleared. The word can also be an execution: when Jehu came to Jezreel, he said, Throw her down. So they threw her down: and some of her blood was sprinkled on the wall (2 Kings 9:33), fulfilling to the letter what Elijah had spoken years before. And our Lord uses it of the temple itself, of which He said that there should not be left one stone upon another that shall not be thrown down (Matthew 24:2).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines THROW as to fling, cast, or hurl; to drive or send by force; to overturn or prostrate; and, of a building, to demolish or cast down.
webster_full: THROW, v.t. — To fling; to cast; to hurl; to drive or send to a distance from the hand or from an engine.
To overturn; to prostrate in wrestling; to lay flat.
To cast down; to demolish; as, to throw down a wall.
To venture at dice; to cast, as lots.
Anglo-Saxon thrawan, to twist, to hurl — the same root as thread and throe.
scriptures: Judges 6:25

And it came to pass the same night, that the LORD said unto him, Take thy father's young bullock, even the second bullock of seven years old, and throw down the altar of Baal that thy father hath, and cut down the grove that is by it:
Jeremiah 1:10
See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant.
2 Kings 9:33
And he said, Throw her down. So they threw her down: and some of her blood was sprinkled on the wall, and on the horses: and he trode her under foot.
Matthew 24:2
And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.
corruption_summary: Jeremiah 1:10 puts four verbs of demolition before two of construction, which cuts against the widespread assumption that a ministry is faithful only insofar as it is relentlessly positive.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah is set over nations to root out, pull down, destroy and throw down before he is told to build and plant. The proportion is deliberate and it is repeated across the prophets. A pulpit that has no negative office — that never names an error, never dismantles a false confidence, never tells a congregation what must go — is not more gracious than Jeremiah’s, it is less biblical. Paul gives the same shape to the pastoral charge: the elder must be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers (Titus 1:9), and the weapons of the Christian warfare are for casting down imaginations (2 Corinthians 10:5). The building is real and it is the goal; but the site is cleared first, and a ministry that will not clear ground is building on an altar of Baal.

Gideon’s commission is worth pressing because of whose altar it was. Not the Midianites’ — the altar of Baal that thy father hath. The first act of the deliverer is against the idolatry of his own household, at night, in fear, and it nearly costs him his life the next morning. Reformation that begins abroad and never comes home is not reformation. The Puritans applied this to the family with a directness the modern church has lost: the head of a household is responsible for what is worshipped under his roof, and the fifth commandment does not oblige a son to maintain his father’s idols. Gideon threw the altar down and built a proper one in its place, which is the whole pattern in a single night.
roots_summary: Hebrew harac (H2040), to throw down or break down; nathats (H5422), to pull down, to demolish; shamat (H8058), to let fall; Greek kataluo (G2647), to throw down, to dissolve.
roots_lines: Hebrew harac (H2040) — to throw down, to break down; throw down the altar of Baal (Judges 6:25).
Hebrew nathats (H5422) — to pull down or demolish, used across the reformation narratives of Kings and Chronicles.
Hebrew shamat (H8058) — to let drop or throw down; Jehu’s order concerning Jezebel (2 Kings 9:33).
Greek kataluo (G2647) — to loosen down, to demolish; that shall not be thrown down (Matthew 24:2).
Greek kathairesis (G2506) — a pulling down; the purpose of the believer’s weapons in 2 Corinthians 10:4.
usage: Throw down the altar of Baal that thy father hath (Judges 6:25) — reformation begins at home and begins with removal.
To root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant (Jeremiah 1:10) — four verbs of demolition before two of construction.
There shall not be left here one stone upon another (Matthew 24:2) — the temple itself under the same word.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon befeallan, to fall upon or happen to, from be- and feallan, to fall. Webster 1828: to happen to; to occur to; to come to pass. The English word keeps a doctrine in its shape: events fall upon a man, and Scripture is clear about whose hand releases them.
biblical_def: Jacob gathers his sons for the last time with a word that reaches past their lifetimes: Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you that which shall befall you in the last days (Genesis 49:1). What follows is not a father’s hope but prophecy, and it includes the sceptre that shall not depart from Judah. The same verb carries a father’s ordinary dread: But Benjamin, Joseph's brother, Jacob sent not with his brethren; for he said, Lest peradventure mischief befall him (Genesis 42:4) — a fear that was, as the story unfolds, both understandable and unnecessary, since the son he mourned was already governing Egypt. Moses uses it to predict apostasy with painful precision: I know that after my death ye will utterly corrupt yourselves, and turn aside from the way which I have commanded you; and evil will befall you in the latter days (Deuteronomy 31:29). And Paul, going up to Jerusalem with his eyes open, sets the pattern for Christian resolve: I go bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem, not knowing the things that shall befall me there (Acts 20:22). He does not know what will fall on him; he goes anyway, because the next verse tells him only that bonds and afflictions abide him.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BEFALL as to happen to; to occur to; to betide; and intransitively, to come to pass; to happen.
webster_full: BEFALL, v.t. — To happen to; to occur to; as, let me know the worst that can befall me.
BEFALL, v.i. — To come to pass; to happen.
BEFELL, pret. — Happened; came to pass.
BEFALLEN, pp. — Happened; come to pass.
Anglo-Saxon befeallan, from be and feallan, to fall — the event conceived as falling upon a man.
scriptures: Genesis 49:1
And Jacob called unto his sons, and said, Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you that which shall befall you in the last days.
Genesis 42:4
But Benjamin, Joseph's brother, Jacob sent not with his brethren; for he said, Lest peradventure mischief befall him.
Deuteronomy 31:29

For I know that after my death ye will utterly corrupt yourselves, and turn aside from the way which I have commanded you; and evil will befall you in the latter days; because ye will do evil in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger through the work of your hands.
Acts 20:22
And now, behold, I go bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem, not knowing the things that shall befall me there:
corruption_summary: The word makes events sound like accidents falling out of the sky, and Scripture everywhere denies that they are — which is precisely the doctrine open theism and practical fatalism both surrender.
corruption_paragraphs: Befall is an accident-shaped word doing service in a book that has no accidents. Deuteronomy 31:29 shows the grammar: evil will befall Israel because ye will do evil in the sight of the LORD. What falls is neither random nor unattached to moral cause. Proverbs 16:33 puts the same point at the sharpest edge available — the lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD — and Amos 3:6 asks whether there be evil in a city and the LORD hath not done it. Open theism, which denies exhaustive foreknowledge, must treat much of what befalls a man as genuinely undetermined even to God; the practical fatalism of the ordinary heart treats it as undetermined by anyone. The Reformed doctrine of providence rejects both: God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, working all things after the counsel of His own will, yet without being the author of sin and without destroying the will of the creature.

Genesis 42:4 is a small mercy to anyone who has ever feared for a child. Jacob withholds Benjamin against a mischief that never comes, while grieving a son who is at that moment second in Egypt and preparing to save the whole family. His fear was sincere, reasonable, and wrong — not because fear is irrational but because he could not see the providence he was inside of. Genesis 50:20 gives the family’s own verdict on the whole affair: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good. That is the answer to fear about what may befall, and it is not a promise that nothing hard will fall. Paul in Acts 20:22 goes to Jerusalem not knowing, and bonds do await him. The comfort is not in the outcome being pleasant but in the hand being sure.
roots_summary: Hebrew qara (H7122), to encounter or befall; qarah (H7136), to happen or meet; Greek sunantao (G4876), to meet with, to befall.
roots_lines: Hebrew qara (H7122) — to meet, to encounter, to befall; that which shall befall you in the last days (Genesis 49:1).
Hebrew qarah (H7136) — to happen or come to pass; the verb behind mischief befall him (Genesis 42:4).
Greek sunantao (G4876) — to meet with, to befall; the things that shall befall me there (Acts 20:22).
Hebrew ason (H611) — mischief, calamity, hurt; the specific evil Jacob feared (Genesis 42:4).
Hebrew acharith (H319) — the latter end, the last days; the horizon of both Genesis 49:1 and Deuteronomy 31:29.
usage: That which shall befall you in the last days (Genesis 49:1) — not a father’s hope but prophecy.
Lest peradventure mischief befall him (Genesis 42:4) — a fear sincere, reasonable, and wrong.
Not knowing the things that shall befall me there (Acts 20:22) — he does not know, and he goes.
